passage: Counsellor's note, Ramesh, Class 10. Observed at the school talent show rehearsal: Ramesh kept smoothing his hair, tugging his collar and checking his reflection in his phone, glancing at the group of girls near the stage. He also turned his back to the audience whenever anyone laughed. A classmate teased him with "Who are you dressing for?" and Ramesh went red and stopped rehearsing for a bit. I asked him privately how he felt. He said, "I just want to look okay." I told him grooming is ordinary, and the teasing was unkind. I spoke to the class about jokes. Yamini stayed beside him afterwards. Follow up next week.

qa.q: What did Ramesh keep checking his reflection in?
qa.a: He kept checking his reflection in his phone.

qa.q: What was Ramesh feeling when he smoothed his hair and tugged his collar under the gaze of others?
qa.a: He was self-conscious and wanted to look okay, and the classmate's teasing made him more embarrassed. It might also be ordinary grooming before a show.

qa.q: How could the class support a student who adjusts his appearance a lot?
qa.a: Avoid teasing about it and treat grooming as normal, as the counsellor did. A quiet chat and a friend nearby help.

qa.q: How does the classmate's teasing affect Ramesh?
qa.a: It made him blush and stop rehearsing, deepening his insecurity. He may have felt watched even more.

grounding: A teenager adjusts appearance under peer gaze, which shows self-consciousness or grooming, and teasing deepens insecurity.

passage:
At the temple fair in the kasba, Aparna kept stopping at the bangle stall mirror to fix her dupatta and smooth her hair. When a group of boys from her school came near the Ferris wheel, she took out her phone and stared at it, though there was no signal.
Her cousin Darshan grinned. "Getting ready for your fans?"
Aparna's cheeks burned. She tugged the dupatta over her head and turned away.
Darshan saw her face go tight. He stopped grinning. "Hey. Sorry. Something wrong?"
"The wind keeps messing my hair, and those boys laughed at my braces last week," she muttered. "I just don't want them to look."
Darshan stepped to stand between her and the boys. "Then let's go to the jalebi stall. They can't see us there."

qa.q: Where did Aparna keep fixing her dupatta?
qa.a: At the bangle stall mirror.

qa.q: What was Aparna feeling when she stared at her phone?
qa.a: Aparna felt self-conscious and anxious, not wanting the boys who had laughed at her braces to look at her.

qa.q: What did Darshan do that turned it around?
qa.a: He noticed her tight face, stopped teasing, asked what was wrong, and shielded her by moving them away.

qa.q: How did Darshan first read Aparna's grooming?
qa.a: He thought she was preening to look good for the boys, not realising she felt insecure.

grounding: At a village fair, a teenager's adjusting and phone-hiding are read as showing off, but come from self-consciousness, and teasing is stopped.

passage:
In the Manchester school corridor, the class lined up for the yearly photo. Emeka kept tugging his blazer straight, pulling the cuffs down, checking his tie in the glass of the trophy cabinet.
Alejandro rolled his eyes. "Vain much?"
Emeka didn't answer. He tugged the cuffs again.
Alejandro looked closer. The blazer hung off Emeka's shoulders; the sleeves nearly covered his fingers. "Is that... your brother's?"
Emeka nodded, jaw tight. "Mum said I'll grow into it."
Alejandro felt his face go warm. "Sorry. I thought you were just posing."
He reached over and folded Emeka's cuffs back neatly, one turn each. "There. Nobody'll notice."
Emeka checked the glass once more, and this time he stood still.

qa.q: Where did Emeka check his tie?
qa.a: In the glass of the trophy cabinet.

qa.q: What was Emeka feeling while tugging his blazer straight?
qa.a: Emeka felt self-conscious and embarrassed about his oversized hand-me-down blazer, worried it would show in the photo.

qa.q: What did Alejandro do that helped?
qa.a: He looked more closely, apologised for teasing, and quietly folded the cuffs so the blazer fit better.

qa.q: How did Alejandro first read Emeka's adjusting?
qa.a: He thought Emeka was being vain and posing, not realising the blazer was too big.

grounding: Before a school photo, a teenager's constant adjusting is read as vanity but comes from insecurity about a hand-me-down blazer.

passage: In the hostel common room, the new Class 11 batch sat in a circle for the welcome evening. Leela, who had arrived from Shillong that morning, kept tucking the same strand of hair behind her ear, smoothing her kurta, then lifting her phone and staring at the dark screen as if it held something important. When her turn came to introduce herself, Ujjwal called out, "Mirror, mirror on the wall!" A few people laughed. Leela's ears turned red and she mumbled her name so quietly that the warden asked her to repeat it. Ujjwal saw her shoulders fold in and the phone go back up in front of her face. At dinner he slid his tray next to hers. "That was a rubbish joke. First day's hard enough. Shillong, right? Tell me about it?" Leela lowered the phone.

qa.q: Where had Leela arrived from?
qa.a: Shillong.

qa.q: What might Leela's hair-tucking and phone-staring suggest?
qa.a: Leela probably felt self-conscious and nervous on her first evening among strangers, though some of it may have been ordinary grooming.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal repair things?
qa.a: He called his own joke rubbish, said first days are hard, and asked Leela about Shillong, giving her a friendly way in.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal have felt seeing Leela's shoulders fold in?
qa.a: Ujjwal likely felt sorry and uncomfortable, seeing that his joke had deepened her embarrassment.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager fixing hair and hiding behind a phone when watched, and teasing about it deepening her insecurity.
